settings.description: Over 30,000 developers, students and knowledge workers told us how they learn, build, and work.
settings.descriptionLong: Now in it’s sixteenth year the annual Developer Survey provides a crucial snapshot into the needs of the global technology community, focusing on the tools and technologies they use or indeed don’t.

chapters.name: Work
chapters.description: Work is more than just a pay check.  Work is where innovation starts, and answers to technology questions take shape.

questions.name: Relationship to coding
questions.description: 75% code as a primary job function; 91% create code at least occasionally. This survey is for and about a builder audience.

questions.name: Work environment
questions.description: 66% hold bachelor’s or master’s degrees, but 23% have no completed university degree. Formal education is common, not universal.

questions.name: Employment status
questions.description: Employment varies notably by country: Germany 73%, France 71%, USA 69%, India 58%. India also has the highest student share at 19%.

questions.name: Employment additional status
questions.description: Respondents often have overlapping obligations. 18% of employed respondents care for dependents, while substantial numbers combine employment, contracting, or study with additional paid work.

questions.name: Work Setting
questions.description: Geography strongly shapes work arrangements. Remote work is 48% in the USA but 21% in France; India has the largest in-person share at 28%. Germany stands out for employee-controlled flexibility.

questions.name: Industry
questions.description: Most respondents are embedded in industries such as finance, healthcare, retail, education, and government.

questions.name: IC or PM
questions.description: 81% identify as individual contributors, including 30% senior/staff ICs. Only 3% are exclusively people managers

questions.name: Years coding
questions.description: 38% have coded for at least 20 years, and 17% for 30+ years. This is a highly experienced coding population.

questions.name: Title
questions.description: Full-stack and back-end developers comprise 41% of titles.

questions.name: Functions at work
questions.description: The typical role extends far beyond coding: 67% review code, 63% make architecture decisions, 56% document, and 52% deploy.

questions.name: Employer organization size
questions.description: 34% work in organizations under 100 employees, while 30% work in organizations of 1,000+. Another 10% are solo workers.

questions.name: Tech budget decisionmaker status
questions.description: Among respondents who know the answer, budget increases outnumber budget decreases 27% to 21%. However, 32% do not know their department’s budget direction.

questions.name: Relationship to purchase decisions at work
questions.description: 59% influence requirements and 48% evaluate tools, but only 18% make final purchase decisions.

questions.name: Reasons to endorse a technology
questions.description: Reliability is the leading recommendation driver at 17%, followed by productivity at 16%. AI features motivate only 2.3%, below community, developer experience, flexibility, trust, and documentation.

questions.name: Count of tools used
questions.description: 35% report 10+ tools, and 8% report 20+ tools.

questions.description: Just 22% are classified as happy, while 33% are unhappy and 45% are

Reasons job is easy
questions.description: Tools are the largest positive intervention at 20%, yet 21% say nothing made work easier. Supportive colleagues follow at 17%, showing that technical and human enablement matter similarly.

questions.name: Does AI affect job ease
questions.description: AI is tightly associated with tool access: 68% say it was the main reason tools made work easier, and another 26% say it contributed. AI is much less likely to be the main reason supportive teams or clear priorities helped.

questions.name: Does AI affect job difficulties
questions.description: AI is usually not associated with job difficulties at work: the top two reasons users find their job difficult, unclear priorities and inefficient processes, 69% for each say AI was not involved.

chapters.name: Knowledge
chapters.description: Knowledge. Context. Trust.  We dig into how we use it at work and where friction tends to get in the way of a good thing.

questions.name: Time spent finding information
questions.description: ~59% spend 5+ hours/week searching for information; 11% spend 20+ hours

questions.name: Important project context
questions.description: Project goals (85%) and code/technical docs (73%) are the most needed context types.

questions.name: Barriers to finding context
questions.description: Incomplete info (63%), knowledge in people's heads (61%), and outdated info (57%) are top barriers.

questions.name: Managing work context
questions.description: Context management is highly manual — keeping separate notes (54%) and starting fresh AI sessions (45%) dominate.

questions.name: Discovering context too late
questions.description: 79% discover important context only after starting a task, highlighting systemic context gaps.

questions.name: Sources for work-related answers
questions.description: Coworkers (72%) and code repos (63%) are the go-to sources — internal beats external.

questions.name: Importance of information accuracy
questions.description: Accuracy is the expectation for official docs and code repos; chat tools and Stack Overflow face lower accuracy expectations.

questions.name: Importance of current information
questions.description: Recency/timestamps matter most for project tools and code repos; people tolerate stale human knowledge.

questions.name: Importance of source traceability
questions.description: Source traceability is most critical for code repos and API docs; coworker knowledge is trusted by reputation.

questions.name: Source attribution for AI answers
questions.description: 79% consider source attribution important or very important for trusting AI answers.

questions.name: Signals of trustworthy information
questions.description: Recency (72.6%) and authority (60%) beat attribution and peer validation as trust signals.

questions.name: Tasks delegated to AI agents
questions.description: Code tasks dominate AI use (73% write code, 62% debug); critical ops like deploying (10%) are rarely delegated.

questions.name: Control over information used by AI
questions.description: 64% actively curate what info AI uses; 17% have little or no visibility into AI inputs.

questions.name: Factors in AI adoption
questions.description: Output quality, security, and price drive adoption — organizations are pragmatic and risk-averse.

questions.name: Organizational AI usage practices
questions.description: 38% of orgs set AI spending limits; 18% have no formal governance.

questions.name: AI cost and usage limits
questions.description: 33% self-monitor AI usage; cost pressure changes model selection and task selectivity.

questions.name: Cost-conscious prompting
questions.description: 75% changed prompts for quality, 38% for cost — quality optimization outpaces cost-cutting 2:1.

chapters.name: AI
chapters.description: What you thought you knew, and what you never knew, about AI and agents.

questions.name: AI tool usage
questions.description: 83% use at least one AI tool. Coding assistants (66%) and general chat tools (63%) dominate; agents/workflows reach 26%.

questions.name: AI tool usage frequency
questions.description: AI coding assistants have become habitual: 73% of their users use them daily. Internal company tools trail at 48% daily and 21% infrequently.

questions.name: AI tool usage daily
questions.description: Daily use is substantial, not incidental: 55% use AI for at least two hours per day, including 31% at four or more hours.

questions.name: Attitudes towards AI tools
questions.description: Overall sentiment is 62% favorable. It closely tracks frequency: 71% of daily users are favorable, compared with 20% of infrequent users. This is not proof that greater use leads to favorable attitudes, but they are certainly related.

sections.name: Trust in AI and other trends

questions.section: Trust in AI and other trends
questions.name: Trust in AI tools
questions.description: Trust is conditional: 48% trust AI when they can easily verify it, while only 7% trust it with important decisions. Even among daily users, important-decision trust is just 8%.

questions.section: Trust in AI and other trends
questions.name: AI workflow current and expected
questions.description: Adoption centers on familiar-code generation (67%), debugging/refactoring (61%), straightforward questions (56%), and tests (55%). Production operations have the strongest resistance: 33% do not use AI there and do not plan to.

questions.section: Trust in AI and other trends
questions.name: Next steps after receiving an AI prompt response
questions.description: Most developers validate AI output by running it locally (76%), comparing it with the codebase (64%), or checking tests/security (53%). Only 10% use answers as-is.

questions.section: Trust in AI and other trends
questions.name: How good are AI tools at complex tasks
questions.description: Only 16% say AI handles complex tasks very well; 39% say “good, but not great.” Daily users are much more positive, while 45% of infrequent users rate performance bad or very poor.

questions.section: Trust in AI and other trends
questions.name: AI tool count
questions.description: Three-quarters use two to five AI products weekly. Tool proliferation exists, but only 5% use six or more.

questions.name: AI agent data storage tools
questions.description: Mem0 leads at 20%, but no product exceeds one-fifth of the sample, the agent-memory market remains fragmented.

questions.name: AI agent orchestration tools
questions.description: LangChain leads at 30%, followed by OpenAI Agents SDK at 24%. “Terminal Use” at 19% suggests many developers favor direct, lightweight orchestration over dedicated frameworks.

questions.name: AI agent observability and security
questions.description: Sentry leads at 26%, ahead of LangSmith at 17%. Established monitoring products may have an advantage as AI observability converges with conventional application monitoring.

questions.name: AI coding agents
questions.description: Claude Code (66%) and GitHub Copilot (59%) are the clear leaders.

questions.name: AI-no-code agents
questions.description: Lovable leads at 38%, with Replit and v0 near 28%.

questions.name: AI agent automation tools
questions.description: Make (39%) and n8n (33%) lead Zapier (18%). Developer-oriented automation appears to be shifting toward flexible, composable platforms.

questions.name: AI impact in different work functions
questions.description: AI is considered useful or very useful for implementation (74%), debugging (72%), documentation (65%), and review (64%).

questions.name: Satisfaction with AI tools
questions.description: AI most improves satisfaction with debugging (65%), documentation (59%), and implementation (59%). Implementation is also most polarizing: 20% report decreased satisfaction.

questions.name: Did you switch AI tools in the past year?
questions.description: Two-thirds switched tools during the year. Output quality is the largest reason at 25%, well ahead of integration (7%), cost (6%), security (2%), or model access (2%).

questions.name: AI memory retention
questions.description: 54% want personal control of AI memory; only 15% prefer centralized organizational control. Another 14% reject retained memory entirely.

questions.name: AI at work
questions.description: Organizational maturity is uneven. AI is optional and individual-led for 30%; only 24% report approved tools and guidance.

questions.name: AI avoidance
questions.description: 59% intentionally avoid AI for some reason. Skill loss/job replacement (17%) exceeds ethical (15%), privacy/security (13%), environmental (8%), or training concerns (3%).

questions.name: Vetting new AI tools
questions.description: Half of organizations have standardized on one or a few approved tools, while 30% are decentralized or actively experimenting. Only 4% are building internal tools/models.

features.headline: Top used programming languages features Javascript at the top of the list for 12th year in a row
features.description: The majority of developers are using JavaScript, SQL, HTML/CSS, Python, and Bash/Shell. Not too surprising; these are the basic techs involved in web software, and everything is web  software these days. No real complaints here, about a third of folks want to use these techs in 6 months (except for the shell languages (25%) and HTML (29%) because can’t we get a script to write that? ). AI seems to love using JavScript and Python (38% each).

features.headline: What’s new, what’s old, and something for everyone in technologies surveyed this year
features.description: The technology leaderboards have been a constant feature in our Developer Surveys from the beginning. That’s the core of the software developer’s toolkit. What’s changed are the categories of tech on this list: cloud providers, coding agents, LLMs, and security ops.  Many of the top technologies on some of these lists have been there for years. Some lists show clear leaders in the space. But there's still plenty of room for alternative technologies to gain ground: each of these lists includes a long tail of tools in the single digits for usage (and we had to cut the lists off somewhere).
For the most used programming languages, Javascript is at the top of the list for 12th year in a row

features.headline: The Core Stack: Technologies that stand the test of time
features.description:
The majority of developers are using JavaScript, SQL, HTML/CSS, Python, and Bash/Shell. Not too surprising; these are the basic techs involved in web software, and everything is web software these days. No real complaints here, about a third of folks want to use these techs in six6 months (except for the shell languages (25%) and HTML (29%) because can’t we get a script to write that?). AI seems to love using JavScript and Python (38% each).

For the backend (and standalone) languages, things get a little more diversified. Java and C# both top the list at roughly 27%, though C# seems to leave a slightly better impression, as slightly more people want to use it in the next six months. Rust perennially has more admirers than users. Other languages more admired than used include Zig, Haskel, Elixir, and Erlang.
Postgres continues reign as the most used database, used by a majority of respondents.

Postgres continues to rule in the database space. In an interview on [Stack Overflow’s podcast Shireesh Thota](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/02/17/data-is-the-new-oil/) (Corporate VP of Azure Databases at Microsoft) said "I tell everyone that Postgres is the Linux of databases... It's one of the best open source projects out there where the community really rallies. They care deeply."  Is it also the AI gateway drug?  That’s how Brian O'Grady (Head of Field Research at Qdrant) put it when he summarized in a [separate interview](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/05/05/what-un-exactly-do-you-mean-by-semantic-search/) with us the ease of starting with its vector capabilities: "I've called it almost like a gateway drug to vector search. As soon as you use pgvector, you're in."

features.headline: I tell everyone that Postgres is the Linux of databases... It's one of the best open source projects out there where the community really rallies. They care deeply.
features.description: Shireesh Thota, Corporate VP of Azure Databases at Microsoft ([source](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/02/17/data-is-the-new-oil/))

features.headline: Builders are still building in the age of AI
features.description: When developers open their IDEs to build in-house software, popular predictions of an AI-driven "SaaSpocalypse" turn out to be greatly exaggerated. Developers are building at high volumes, but their focus remains on internal utilities and glue code rather than replacing commercial software. 77% of developers build small scripts and automations, while 63% create team-level internal tools.  54% build customer-facing applications—a reminder that a vast portion of engineers work inside traditional enterprise sectors like retail, finance, and manufacturing. Vendor replacement sits at the bottom: Only 19% of respondents build in-house software to replace paid vendors.
Small scripts are most common for builders to work on, 19% say they’re building tools to replace paid vendors.

When cross-referencing these builds with AI tool usage, a subtle trend emerges: AI adoption steadily drops as system complexity and operational risk increase. While 54% of developers replacing vendors utilize AI assistance, this represents a rate only within that specific subgroup. Across the entire survey pool, just 10% of total developers are using AI to replace third-party software. Vendor replacement is far from an AI breakout story—it's actually the workload where AI assistance sees the lowest ceiling for adoption. The survey's AI friction data explains why developers hesitate to replace SaaS vendors with custom LLM-generated software. Paid tools offload security compliance, SLAs, and continuous maintenance. Replacing them transfers technical debt back onto internal teams, right where AI errors create the most pain. Developers are happy to let AI generate low-risk automation scripts, but when it comes to business-critical SaaS, most teams still prefer paying a vendor over managing unmaintainable, AI-generated technical debt.
While only 16% say they’re building tools to replace paid vendors, of that cohort more than half are doing so with the help of AI.

features.headline: Frontier models’ next evolution
features.description: While OpenAI and Anthropic sit neck-and-neck at the top of general LLM usage (74% and 75% adoption, respectively), practitioner sentiment reveals a clear divergence when evaluating developer preference and agentic execution. Anthropic holds a clear lead in forward-looking interest, with 49% of developers expressing a desire to work with Claude over the next six months, compared to 32% for OpenAI. When building autonomous coding agents or complex tool-calling pipelines, developers lean heavily toward Anthropic (45% usage) over OpenAI (32% usage). Spend tracking data from Ramp mirrors this shift, showing Anthropic capturing market share rapidly as engineering teams transition from simple chat interfaces to structured, programmatic agent architectures.
The two companies focused on frontier models are the top two in LLM usage: Anthropic at 75% and OpenAI at 74%.

Disruption and security remain areas for improvement. Few respondents reported working with security technology, suggesting AI security ops is still a relatively isolated field—and possibly a good target for anyone looking to add future-forward tools to their toolkit. Even setting aside dedicated security practitioners, 23% of users said their team lost valuable time to security or privacy issues stemming from AI.
For all the talk of security work shifting left, only 23% of respondents have used security tools in the past year.

questions.name: AI’s impact on Stack Overflow usage

features.headline: 69% use GitHub projects or Stack Overflow as their community platform of choice in the past year
features.description: Public GitHub projects (69%) and Stack Overflow (69%) tied as the most heavily utilized technical community platforms in the past year, followed by YouTube (58%) and Reddit (54%).

features.headline: 52% learned a new skill or programming language in the last year
features.description: Over half of respondents actively began learning to code or acquired a new programming skill in the past year, relying most on technical documentation (59%) and AI codegen tools (53%).

methodology.description: **30,903** responses from **169** countries are used in these survey results.

methodology.headline: Survey felding
methodology.description:
The current local response extract includes 39,266 total rows recorded from June 23, 2026 through August 5, 2026, of which 30,903 are marked as valid responses.

The survey was promoted through stackoverflow.com, stackoverflow.blog and our email list to community members that are opted into learning about research opportunities or announcements.

The survey instrument should be referenced from the public Stack Exchange survey repository: [StackExchange/Survey](https://github.com/StackExchange/Survey).

The public call for feedback that informed the 2026 Developer Survey should be referenced from Meta Stack Overflow: [Help shape the 2026 Developer Survey](https://meta.stackoverflow.com/questions/438884/help-shape-the-2026-developer-survey).

methodology.headline: Valid responses
methodology.description:
The current valid-response rule is implemented in `mark_valid_responses()` in `R/aggregation.R`. At a high level, the function adds an integer `valid_response` indicator to the response data.

When bot exclusion is enabled and the input data does not already include `is_bot`, the function first runs `flag_bots()`. The current bot flag uses Qualtrics response-quality fields, including reCAPTCHA score, duplicate respondent status, straightlining questions, unanswered questions, progress, duration, and whether `Country` was answered.

Responses are marked valid through either the primary inclusion rule or the substantive-response recovery rule.

Primary inclusion rule:

- `Consent` is present and equals `"I agree"`.
- `Employment` is present.
- The response is not flagged as a bot when bot exclusion is enabled.

Substantive-response recovery rule:

- The response answered all ten core fielding questions listed below.
- This recovery rule is evaluated independently of the primary non-bot condition, so a response with `is_bot == TRUE` can still receive `valid_response == 1` when it answered all ten core fielding questions.

Core fielding questions:

- `Country`
- `Currency`
- `Compensation`
- `TechDropDown`
- `Languages`
- `CodeTest`
- `Databases`
- `CloudPlat`
- `WebFramework`
- `DevIDE`

The survey-section scripts use `valid_response == 1` as the inclusion rule for exports, so the substantive-response recovery rule is preserved downstream.

methodology.headline: Write-in handling
methodology.description:
Role write-ins from `Role_38_TEXT` are reviewed only among `valid_response == 1` responses, normalized to group repeated answers, and compared against existing and analyst-approved Role categories. Reviewed matches can recode `"Other, please specify"` into a final Role category while retaining `Role_Original` and `Role_NLP_Status`; unresolved write-ins remain grouped as `"Other"` in summaries.

SOChangeAddl written responses are eligible for public use only when `valid_response == 1`, `SOChangeAddlConsent` gives permission to share publicly, and `SOChangeAddl` is non-empty. Responses are decoded, translated to English when needed, and manually curated with `SOChangeAddlPublishText`, `SOChangeAddlInclude`, and `SOChangeAddlExcludeReason`; automated text flags are used only to support review, not to make final publish decisions.

methodology.headline: Compensation handling
methodology.description: Compensation is analyzed among `valid_response == 1` responses with non-missing `Country`, `Currency`, and positive numeric `Compensation`; values are converted to yearly USD using exchange rates, with a documented Ukraine-specific correction when likely USD values were entered under `UAH`. Compensation statistics and charts use rows where `CompensationStatsInclude` and `CompensationChartInclude` are `TRUE`, excluding rows with multiple quality flags such as very low or very high converted values, country outliers, suspicious raw-number patterns, non-employed respondents, or student/retired roles.
